Bishop's Hill fully demolished, residents did not protest

Mr. So said he received the demolition notice at the end of July and immediately approached Sham Shui Po district councillors to reflect his wish to retain the fitness facilities on Wozai Mountain, but he quoted their reply as saying "none of the equipment will be preserved." Mr. So said that in the past, whenever faced with demolition, they had been able to organise residents to petition and protest, but this time the notification period was too short and there was insufficient time to organise residents to stop the works. As a result, the popular morning exercise spot of more than 20 years will finally bid farewell.

Three days ago (10th), the Home Affairs Department announced the Wozai Mountain improvement plan. The government will clear illegal and unsafe structures, facilities or杂物 on the mountain in phases, stating that the relevant objects have been illegally occupying government land for many years.

Yesterday (12th), at around 6:30 a.m., staff from the Lands Department and uniformed police arrived at the scene, cordoning off the area from the foot to the top of the Tong Yam Street hillside rest garden. Porters then arrived to remove fitness equipment, bicycles, ping-pong tables and other items. Police deployed冲锋车 and猪笼车 to stand guard. Mr. So said this is just a place where residents exercise, and he does not understand the purpose of the police arrangement: "The officers are standing here, monitoring us the whole time. What have we done? Are we rioters? Have we broken the law?"

From "morning exercise hotspot" to LCSD facilities

Mr. So said residents crowdfunded a total of HK$400,000 to build the "morning exercise hotspot" on Bishop's Hill, including ping-pong tables, fitness equipment, and an unofficial hiking trail built decades ago. On the day of demolition, many residents were still doing morning exercises and using the fitness facilities. Several residents said they were deeply saddened by the disappearance of a place where they had exercised for years. Some residents kept asking Mr. So what to do, but he was also at a loss.

He said he has been moving the fitness equipment away over the past few days, hoping to preserve as much as possible the fruits of his own labour. So far, he has removed all the muscle massage rollers, while some residents want to move parts of the religious statues to Lantau Island.

According to the Home Affairs Department's Wozai Mountain improvement plan, the "morning exercise hotspot" will be converted into LCSD facilities. The makeshift fitness equipment on the mountain will be replaced by standard leisure and sports facilities provided by the LCSD; as for the religious statues, religious leaders will handle them properly on site.

Surviving against the odds, building Bishop's Hill "morning exercise hotspot"

75-year-old So Chi-keung is a SARS survivor. Due to side effects of medication, he suffered后遗症 such as muscle pain, weakness and fatigue. After three years of physiotherapy, his condition had not improved. In 2008, invited by a neighbour, So went to Bishop's Hill. After morning exercise, he found his spirits improved, which he attributed to the fresh mountain air. He then began exercising on Bishop's Hill every morning at six. After persisting for a month, his health and strength returned, and he decided to stop physiotherapy.

In 2009, Mr. So travelled to South Korea and was inspired by the fitness facilities there. Back in Hong Kong, he designed and "homemade" a stationary bike and a cable machine at his own hardware factory, then single-handedly carried the equipment up Bishop's Hill in pieces. He described the making process as simple but the transportation up the mountain as extremely difficult. Over four years, he built more than 20 fitness facilities on Bishop's Hill, including swings, balance bars and rollers, and placed them on the open space above the current Sham Shui Po service reservoir. At the time, some elderly people objected, but later residents who used the facilities found relief from aches and pains, making the equipment very popular.

Bishop's Hill revealed for the first time, residents protest against demolition

Mr. So said that in 2014, more than 200 young people held a psychedelic party on Bishop's Hill, causing noise nuisance. When police arrived, they discovered for the first time a large number of private fitness facilities. The Water Supplies Department subsequently stepped up patrols of Bishop's Hill and repeatedly drove away residents exercising there, and planned to demolish the facilities. At that time, Mr. So organised several protest activities and went in person to the Sham Shui Po District Council Secretariat to fight for the retention of the fitness area.

Accidental check-in, Bishop's Hill reservoir becomes Grade 1 historic building

In 2017, the Water Supplies Department intended to clear the unauthorised structures on Bishop's Hill and return the land to the Lands Department. In addition, the roots of two large trees on top of the reservoir had extended into the interior, posing a collapse risk. In 2020, preparations were made to remove the large trees and fill in the service reservoir. The Water Supplies Department promised Mr. So that his fitness facilities could be placed on the open space after filling, so Mr. So agreed to the works.

As a result, on Christmas Eve, Mr. So and a volunteer sneaked into the reservoir to check if anything had been left behind, and posted photos on social media. The post attracted large crowds to check in at the reservoir and aroused public concern. Mr. So said members of the public protested against the demolition of the reservoir because of its historical value. One regular visitor to Bishop's Hill, Sister Fong, even stood in front of an excavator to stop the demolition works.

In 2021, the reservoir was graded as a Grade 1 historic building by the Antiquities Advisory Committee. The reservoir was preserved and opened to the public. Mr. So moved his fitness facilities to the foot of the hill.

Mao Zedong statue incident may have triggered demolition

In June 2022, the Sham Shui Po District Management Committee intended to remove the shrine and fitness facilities. Mr. So initiated a petition to fight for retention, saying that a total of 3,399 Sham Shui Po district residents signed, and the letter was submitted to the Home Affairs Department, with a promise not to expand the facilities further.

Mr. So said that after that, Bishop's Hill remained stable, with no indication from the government that a clearance was necessary. However, at the beginning of 2026, resident Sister Fong erected a Mao Zedong statue and a Mao Zedong cultural hall on Bishop's Hill. Although the statue was later removed, Mr. So believes the Mao Zedong incident rekindled the government's attention to Bishop's Hill. Coupled with some residents making loud noises on the mountain and disturbing nearby residents, this led the government to decide on a full clearance of Bishop's Hill.

In early 2026, resident Sister Fong set up a Mao Zedong statue and a Mao Zedong cultural hall on Bishop's Hill, reigniting controversy over the use of the site. (File photo)

"Without Bishop's Hill, I would have lived 20 years less"

Watching workers dismantle the fitness equipment he had built piece by piece, Mr. So did not show sadness. He planned to bring the dismantled equipment back to his ancestral home, and kept telling the media the history of Bishop's Hill. In fact, he knows well that Bishop's Hill has been full of controversy, and the "morning exercise hotspot" has been in breach of regulations for years. However, he believes the place has benefited many residents. He hopes that by telling the story of Bishop's Hill, he can gain government recognition. Although the site ultimately cannot be retained, he still wants to pass on the story to repay the grace Bishop's Hill has shown him.

He bid farewell to Bishop's Hill: "I am grateful it gave me a new life. Without it, I would have lost 20 years — I should have died. If not for Bishop's Hill, I would have died……. Besides, I am a SARS survivor who has been hurt. Would I have survived to today?"
